title: Search inside a booking product
metaTitle: Search that returns a bookable time
excerpt: Guests search a booking product when the service list fails them. Show bookable matches in their words, on the phone, and a way back that keeps the time they already chose.
alt: Pale blue and orange ink swirls on a white ground, a surface where the eye looks for one clear shape.
caption: The guest is looking for one shape they already have a name for. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When does a guest search instead of browsing services?
faqs.answer: They search when the list failed. The categories use internal names, the link dropped them in the wrong location, or they remember a treatment, a person, or a room and cannot see it. Search is the repair. Treat it as part of the booking, not as a help-center feature.

faqs.question: What should a booking search result contain?
faqs.answer: A result should be something they can act on: a service with the next open time, a staff member with the next open time, or a location. Use the public name, the duration, and whether they can book it. A blog post about the service is not a booking result unless they asked a question. Hurried guests need a time, not an article.

faqs.question: What if the search has no open times?
faqs.answer: Repeat their words and say there is no open time under that name. Show the next date that does have one, or the nearest public name if they typed a nickname. Do not fill the screen with unrelated services and call it helpful. Keep a way back to the time or location they had already selected.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Booking product search UX is the repair when navigation failed a guest who is on a phone and in a hurry. They typed a service, a person, or a place because the list did not show it. Show matches in their language, and give them a way back to the time they may already have touched.

If the results are internal package names, they will think you do not offer the thing they were told about. They will leave. The booking they would have made becomes a message to the front desk, which is the slower product you were trying to replace.

## They search because the list failed

The service list failed when it was grouped by your org chart. "Tier 2" is not a thing a guest says. "Intro call" is. The location list failed when it opened on the wrong city because a default was convenient for the studio. The staff list failed when it was a wall of photos with first names only and they were given a surname in a text.

Put search where a thumb can reach it on the first screen of the list, not inside a help icon. A single field is enough. Placeholder text can name an example they would type. The placeholder is not a label. The field still needs a real label, because placeholders vanish when they type, and a hurried person needs to know what the box is for.

Do not ask them to pick a category before they can search. The category was the navigation that failed. Search across the services, people, and locations they are allowed to see. Narrowing can come after they see hits.

Jakob Nielsen reported that people often leave a page in 10 to 20 seconds unless the value is clear at once. A search screen that opens with tips, recent posts, and a map, and only then shows a match, spends that window on chrome. [How long people stay on a page](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) argues for rows that look like bookings, immediately, in the words they just typed.

## Matches they can book

A good result is a bookable object. The service name they recognize. How long it takes. The next open time in their timezone. A tap that selects it. If a person is the way you book, the person and their next time. If a location matters, the location and a way to see its times.

Lead with that, not with an article, a policy, or an Instagram image. Content can sit under the bookable hits, labeled as something other than a time, if you must include it. It should not outrank a service that matched the query. A guest who searches "intro call" and gets a journal entry about introductions will assume the calendar is elsewhere.

Use their synonyms. Cut, trim, and the official name of the service should land on the same object if that is how clients talk. You do not need a thesaurus for the whole language. You need the handful of words the front desk already hears. Ask the front desk. Put those words on the service as search text, without displaying the ugly list to the guest.

Show the match in the row. If they typed a staff surname, the surname should be visible, not cropped into an avatar. If they typed a neighborhood, the neighborhood should be on the location row. Highlight is optional. Visible text is not.

Say when they cannot book a hit. A members-only service can appear if they searched its name, with the same reason you use on the service page. Hiding it makes the search look empty. Showing it as if it were open makes the next step a surprise error. The row can say Members, and the tap can explain the path.

## A way back that keeps their place

The query stays in the field. They will edit it. Clearing it on submit makes them retype with a thumb on a pavement. That is a good way to lose the booking.

If they had already selected a location or a time, search must not throw that away without a warning. A common disaster: they pick Thursday, they search to confirm the service name, and the Thursday is gone when they return. Keep the selection. Show it above the results. Let them clear it on purpose.

Name the way back. "Back to Thursday at 9:00" is a landmark. "Back" is a coin flip. If there was no selection, the way back is the list they came from, at the same scroll position if you can manage it. Dropping them at the top of a long list is how they lose the service they had finally found by scrolling, which is why they searched in the first place.

If you offer a correction, show it as an offer. "Search 'intro call' instead." Leave their typed words in the field until they accept. Silent replacement hides misses and looks like you did not listen. A hurried person notices that faster than a calm one, because they remember exactly what they typed.

Recent searches are useful and sensitive. A shared family phone should not announce last week's appointment type in the field's history if that type is private. Prefer a short list they can clear, or keep it only for the session. Do not sync a health or legal service name to another device for the sake of convenience.

## Nothing matched

Repeat the query. "Nothing bookable matches 'beard sculpt.'" Then, if you have a near service, name it as a near service, not as a fake hit. "Closest: Beard trim, next time Friday at 2." They can accept or edit.

If the name is right and the times are the problem, say that. "Intro call is bookable. Nothing is open this week. Next time: Monday at 9:00." That is a successful search with a thin calendar. Do not call it zero results.

If the miss is a location, offer the other locations in plain text. Do not drop a map as the only answer. Maps are hard to operate one-handed, and a pin with no label fails the same test as a color with no word.

Do not backfill the empty screen with your most expensive services. It reads as a trick. The guest needed a specific thing. Showing them an unrelated premium slot is how a search box becomes an ad unit. They will not use it twice.

If a private service exists and they cannot see it, do not hint that it exists unless your policy is to invite them in. "Nothing you can book matches that" is the safe sentence. Leaking a staff-only block through search is a permission bug with a search icon on it.


## Filters, locations, and the wrong city

A guest in a hurry often searches because the page opened on the wrong city. The result row has to name the city in text, not only as a pin. If two studios offer the same service name, the city is the difference, and it belongs on the first line of the row. Making them open a detail page to discover they are about to book in another town wastes the only minute they had.

Offer a location switch that keeps the query. Changing city should rerun the same words. Clearing the service name because they changed city makes them search twice. They will not. They will call the desk and dictate the booking to a person, which is the slower product this screen was supposed to replace.

Date is the other filter worth having, and it can be a single control. This week, and any time, cover the hurried case. A panel of duration, price, staff seniority, and room type is a second product. Put duration and price on the result itself so they can judge the hit without opening a filter sheet they must then dismiss with the same thumb.

If the business has one location, do not show a location filter at all. An empty control is not a sign of a serious system. It is a question they cannot answer, and it steals the first seconds of the results, which are the seconds in which they decide the search failed them again.
## Review the lookups the desk already hears

Collect five phrases from the person who answers the phone. A nickname for a service. A staff surname. A neighborhood. A misspelling you see in texts. A service you no longer offer.

Run them on a phone as a logged-out guest. Each result should be bookable or honestly closed. The query should survive a trip into a service and back. A selected time, if they had one, should survive too.

Watch the first second of results. If a spinner replaces the whole screen, including the field, they cannot even correct a typo while you search. Keep the field stable. Fill rows under it.

Settings are the cabinet next to this. Timezone, reminders, and who the booking is for should not require a hunt, and they should not be a second product. That piece is [settings in a booking product](/blog/settings-in-a-booking-product). Search that ignores the timezone they set will show the right service at the wrong hour, which they will experience as a broken result.

If the booking flow needs a search that returns a time rather than a page, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The list, the result, and the way back are one job. A guest in a hurry will not do that job twice.
